title: Notation
body_md: Throughout, $d$ is the dimension of the data and all asymptotic statements are as $d\to\infty$. We write $a\asymp b$ for bounds in both directions by positive constants independent of $d$, $a\sim b$ for $a/b\to1$, and $\widetilde\Theta$ for order up to polylogarithmic factors.

label: ass:de
title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{ass:de}
Let $\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm TE}$ and $\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm ST}(t)$ be the deterministic equivalents defined in \eqref{eq:main-teacher} and \eqref{eq:main-two-term} below, and let $(T_d)$ be any of the stopping-time sequences appearing in our statements. The random population losses of the ReLU model on the sphere satisfy, in probability as $d\to\infty$,
\[
\mathcal L_{\rm TE}/\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm TE}\to1,
\qquad \mathcal L_{\rm ST}(T_d)/\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm ST}(T_d)\to1.
\]
For statements uniform over stopping times or target families, the corresponding relative approximation is assumed uniform.

name: Deterministic-equivalent teacher error

title: Proof
body_md:
In fact, by \eqref{eq:approxLTE} and Definition~\ref{def:deterministic-resolvent}, we have
\[
    \overline{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{TE}}
    =-\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_\Gamma
    \langle\Psi^{1/2}\beta,(-\Psi\kappa(z)-zI)^{-1}\Psi^{1/2}\beta\rangle\,dz.
\]
We claim that $\kappa$ is holomorphic near $0$, with $\kappa(0)=0$, and that
$\kappa(z)=cz+O(z^2)$ with $c=\nu^{-1}$. To see this, let us write $\kappa(z)=zc(z)$. Substituting this into \eqref{eq:selfconsistentm} gives, for $z\neq0$,
\[
\begin{split}
    -zc(z)
    &=\left(1-\frac{1}{mz}\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Psi(I+c(z)\Psi)^{-1}\bigr)\right)^{-1},\\
    -mzc(z)+c(z)\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Psi(I+c(z)\Psi)^{-1}\bigr)
    &=m.
\end{split}
\]
Thus, the equation becomes
\[
    m=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(c(z)\Psi(I+c(z)\Psi)^{-1}\bigr)-mzc(z).
\]
At $z=0$, this gives
\[
    m=c(0)\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Psi(I+c(0)\Psi)^{-1}\bigr),
\]
such that identifying $c(0)=\nu^{-1}$ gives exactly \eqref{eq:nuequation}, as we wanted. To justify the expansion near zero, observe that
\[
    \left.\frac{d}{dc}\operatorname{tr}\bigl(c\Psi(I+c\Psi)^{-1}\bigr)\right|_{c=\nu^{-1}}
    =\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Psi(I+\nu^{-1}\Psi)^{-2}\bigr)>0.
\]
The analytic implicit function theorem therefore gives a local analytic solution
$c(z)=\nu^{-1}+O(z)$. Since $\kappa(z)=z/\nu+O(z^2)$ has positive imaginary part just above zero, it agrees with the branch in Definition~\ref{def:deterministic-resolvent}. We conclude that $\kappa(z)=cz+O(z^2)$ with $c=\nu^{-1}$, such that
\[
    \overline{R}(z)
    =-\frac{1}{z}(I+\nu^{-1}\Psi)^{-1}+O(1).
\]
Finally, substituting this expansion into \eqref{eq:approxLTE} and integrating in $z$ gives
\[
    \overline{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{TE}}
    =\langle\Psi^{1/2}\beta,(I+\nu^{-1}\Psi)^{-1}\Psi^{1/2}\beta\rangle
    =\nu\langle\Psi^{1/2}\beta,(\Psi+\nu I)^{-1}\Psi^{1/2}\beta\rangle.
\]
as claimed.

label: def:perturbed-resolvent
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:perturbed-resolvent}
For $S=(I-e^{-\Psi t})^2$, let
\[
    \overline{R}_\epsilon(z)
    =(\epsilon S-zI-\Psi\kappa_\epsilon(z))^{-1},
    \qquad
    -\kappa_\epsilon(z)
    =\left(1+\frac{1}{m}\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\Psi\overline{R}_\epsilon(z)\bigr)\right)^{-1}.
\]
For $z$ off the deterministic spectrum, we take the branch analytic in $\epsilon$ near zero that continues Definition~\ref{def:deterministic-resolvent}, so that $\overline{R}_0=\overline{R}$ and $\kappa_0=\kappa$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:double-resolvent-definition}
    \overline{Q}_S(z)
    \coloneqq-\left.\frac{\partial\overline{R}_\epsilon(z)}{\partial\epsilon}\right|_{\epsilon=0},
    \qquad
    \overline{\mathcal{P}}(S)
    \coloneqq\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_\Gamma z\,\overline{Q}_S(z)\,dz,
\end{equation}
where $\Gamma$ is a sufficiently small positively oriented contour around zero. These are the deterministic counterparts of $R(z)SR(z)$ and $P_0SP_0$, respectively.

label: lem:mixed-nu-consequences
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Consequences of the order of $\nu$

title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Items~(i) and~(ii).} By Lemma~\ref{lem:nu-relu}, $\nu\asymp d^{-\alpha-1}$, while $\sigma_k^2\asymp d^{-k-1}$ for fixed $k$. Hence
\[
\frac{\sigma_k^2}{\nu}\asymp d^{\alpha-k},
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{\nu}{\sigma_k^2+\nu}=\frac1{1+\sigma_k^2/\nu}.
\]
If $k<\alpha$ the ratio $\sigma_k^2/\nu$ tends to infinity, and the right-hand side is $\asymp\nu/\sigma_k^2\asymp d^{k-\alpha}$, which is~(i). If $k>\alpha$ the ratio tends to zero, and the right-hand side tends to one, which is~(ii).

\emph{Item~(iii).} The degree-one term alone gives the lower bound, by \eqref{eq:N1sigma1squared}:
\[
\operatorname{tr}\Psi=\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}N_k\sigma_k^2\ \ge\ N_1\sigma_1^2=\frac1{4d}.
\]
For the upper bound, the trace of the kernel operator is the expectation of its diagonal, and $(r)_+^2\le r^2$:
\[
\operatorname{tr}\Psi=\mathbb E_x\,K(x,x)=\mathbb E\,(\langle u,x\rangle)_+^2\ \le\ \mathbb E\,\langle u,x\rangle^2=\frac1d .
\]

\emph{Item~(iv), upper bound.} Since $\frac{\nu\sigma_k^2}{(\sigma_k^2+\nu)^2}\le\frac{\sigma_k^2}{\sigma_k^2+\nu}$ for every $k$, the fixed-point equation \eqref{eq:main-fixed-point} gives
\[
\nu\operatorname{tr}[\Psi(\Psi+\nu I)^{-2}]
=\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}N_k\frac{\nu\sigma_k^2}{(\sigma_k^2+\nu)^2}
\ \le\ \sum_{k\in\mathcal K}N_k\frac{\sigma_k^2}{\sigma_k^2+\nu}=m .
\]

\emph{Item~(iv), lower bound.} Let $J$ be the largest degree in $\mathcal K$ with $J\le\alpha$, and let $D_J=\sum_{k\le J}N_k\asymp d^J$ be the number of eigenvalues of $\Psi$ of degree at most $J$. The first degree in $\mathcal K$ above $J$ exceeds $\alpha$, and $\sigma_k^2$ decreases in $k$ (Claim~\ref{eq:lemmasigmadecreasing}), so by Lemma~\ref{lem:nu-relu}
\[
\sup_{k>J}\frac{\sigma_k^2}{\nu}\longrightarrow0,
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad
\inf_{k>J}\frac{\nu}{\sigma_k^2+\nu}\ \ge\ 1-o(1).
\]
We bound the trace from below by retaining the degrees above $J$ and dropping the degrees up to $J$, which is valid because every summand is nonnegative:
\[
\nu\operatorname{tr}[\Psi(\Psi+\nu I)^{-2}]
=\sum_{k\in\mathcal K}N_k\,\frac{\sigma_k^2}{\sigma_k^2+\nu}\,\frac{\nu}{\sigma_k^2+\nu}
\ \ge\ (1-o(1))\sum_{k>J}N_k\frac{\sigma_k^2}{\sigma_k^2+\nu}.
\]
By the fixed-point equation \eqref{eq:main-fixed-point}, the last sum is $m$ minus the sum over $k\le J$, and each summand there is at most $N_k$:
\[
\sum_{k>J}N_k\frac{\sigma_k^2}{\sigma_k^2+\nu}\ \ge\ m-D_J .
\]
Finally, $D_J/m\to0$ if $J<\alpha$, since $D_J\asymp d^J$, and $D_J/m\to1/J!\le\frac12$ if $J=\alpha\ge2$, by \eqref{eq:Nkasymptotics}. In both cases $m-D_J\gtrsim m$, which completes the proof.

label: prop:mixed-timing

head: environment
name: No quadratic improvement at any stopping time

title: Proof
body_md:
Here $\alpha=5$, and Lemmas~\ref{lem:nu-relu} and~\ref{lem:mixed-nu-consequences} give
\[
\nu\asymp d^{-6},\qquad
\frac{\nu}{\sigma_2^2+\nu}\asymp d^{-3},\qquad
\frac{\nu}{\sigma_4^2+\nu}\asymp d^{-1},\qquad
\nu\operatorname{tr}[\Psi(\Psi+\nu I)^{-2}]\asymp d^{5}.
\]
By \eqref{eq:mixed-additivity}, $\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm TE}=(1-w_d)\frac{\nu}{\sigma_2^2+\nu}+w_d\frac{\nu}{\sigma_4^2+\nu}\asymp d^{-3}$, the second summand being of order $d^{-6}$.

\emph{Lower bound.} Fix $t\ge0$ and write $x=\sigma_4^2t$. We bound $\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm ST}(t)$ from below by retaining two terms of \eqref{eq:mixed-additivity}--\eqref{eq:mixed-unit-de} and dropping all the others, which is valid because every term is nonnegative. The first retained term is the degree-four bias, in which $\frac{\nu+\sigma_4^2e^{-x}}{\sigma_4^2+\nu}\ge\frac{(\nu+\sigma_4^2)e^{-x}}{\sigma_4^2+\nu}=e^{-x}$, so
\[
w_d\,\overline\ell_4(t)\ \ge\ w_d\,e^{-2x}.
\]
The second retained term is the degree-two variance, which we bound from below by retaining only the degree-four summand of the numerator trace of $\overline H$ and dropping the other summands, again valid because they are nonnegative:
\[
(1-w_d)\,\overline\ell_2(t)\ \ge\ (1-w_d)\,\frac{\nu\sigma_2^2}{(\sigma_2^2+\nu)^2}\,
\frac{N_4\,\frac{\nu\sigma_4^2}{(\sigma_4^2+\nu)^2}}{\nu\operatorname{tr}[\Psi(\Psi+\nu I)^{-2}]}\,(1-e^{-x})^2
=:A_d\,(1-e^{-x})^2,
\]
where, by the estimates above and $N_4\asymp d^4$,
\[
A_d\asymp d^{-3}\cdot\frac{d^{4}\cdot d^{-1}}{d^{5}}=d^{-5}.
\]
Combining the two retained terms, for every $t\ge0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mixed-timing-envelope}
\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm ST}(t)\ \ge\ w_d\,e^{-2x}+A_d\,(1-e^{-x})^2
\ \ge\ \min_{0\le y\le1}\bigl[w_dy^2+A_d(1-y)^2\bigr]
=\frac{w_dA_d}{w_d+A_d}\ \asymp\ d^{-5},
\end{equation}
since $w_d$ and $A_d$ are both of order $d^{-5}$. The minimum over $y=e^{-x}$ is computed by completing the square.

\emph{Upper bound.} Let $t=x/\sigma_4^2$ with $x>0$ fixed. The degree-four component contributes at most $\frac54w_d\lesssim d^{-5}$. For the degree-two component, $\sigma_2^2t=x\sigma_2^2/\sigma_4^2\asymp xd^2$, so the exponential in its bias is negligible and the bias is $\asymp\bigl(\frac{\nu}{\sigma_2^2+\nu}\bigr)^2\asymp d^{-6}$; its variance is at most $\frac{\nu}{\sigma_2^2+\nu}\overline H(t)\lesssim d^{-3}(1+x^2)d^{-2}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:mixed-filter} with $j=4$. Hence $\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm ST}(x/\sigma_4^2)\lesssim d^{-5}$, which with \eqref{eq:mixed-timing-envelope} proves \eqref{eq:mixed-timing-orders}; \eqref{eq:mixed-timing-ratios} follows by division.

The figures of this appendix, Figure~\ref{fig:illustrative-time-relative} and Figure~\ref{fig:mixed-target-time-curves} use the particular values $c=(\pi-3)/2$ and $B=C^2/24$ with $C=(12\pi-37)/24$, for which the two competing error terms in each example are equal at leading order, and they are normalized by the leading constants listed in Table~\ref{tab:mixed-constants}. label: lem:general-coefficients
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Harmonic and Hermite coefficients

label: eq:general-Nksigmak
title: Proof
body_md:
The polynomials $h_k=\sqrt{N_k}\,P_k$ are orthonormal for the law of $t$, and by \eqref{eq:general-sigmak}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-Nksigmak}
N_k\sigma_k^2=\bigl(\mathbb E[\sigma(\sqrt d\,t)\,h_k(t)]\bigr)^2 .
\end{equation}
In words, $N_k\sigma_k^2$ is the squared $k$-th coefficient of $\sigma(\sqrt d\,\cdot)$ in the orthonormal polynomials of the law of $t$, while $c_k^2$ is the squared $k$-th coefficient of $\sigma$ in the orthonormal polynomials of the Gaussian.

\emph{(i)} The first equality holds because $\Psi$ has blocks $\sigma_k^2I_{N_k}$. The law of $t$ has compact support, so polynomials are dense in its $L^2$ space and $(h_k)_{k\ge0}$ is an orthonormal basis. The second equality is therefore Parseval's identity, by \eqref{eq:general-Nksigmak}. For the limit, $\sqrt d\,t$ has the density
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-density}
\rho_d(z)=\kappa_d\Bigl(1-\frac{z^2}{d}\Bigr)^{\frac{d-3}{2}},\qquad |z|<\sqrt d,
\end{equation}
where $\kappa_d$ is a normalizing constant. Since $\log(1-y)\le-y$, we have $\rho_d(z)\le Ce^{-z^2/4}$ for $d\ge6$, and $\rho_d$ converges pointwise to the standard Gaussian density. By dominated convergence,
\[
\mathbb E\bigl[g(\sqrt d\,t)\bigr]\ \longrightarrow\ \mathbb E[g(z)]\qquad\text{for every $g$ with }|g(r)|\le Ce^{C|r|},
\]
and in particular for $g=\sigma^2$.

\emph{(ii)} In the variable $z=\sqrt d\,t$, the polynomial $h_k(z/\sqrt d)$ is the degree-$k$ orthonormal polynomial of $\rho_d$ with positive leading coefficient. It is obtained from $1,z,\dots,z^k$ by Gram--Schmidt, so its coefficients are continuous functions of the moments of $\rho_d$ of order at most $2k$, as long as the moment matrix is nonsingular. By the dominated convergence in (i), these moments converge to those of the Gaussian, whose moment matrix is positive definite. Hence the coefficients of $h_k(z/\sqrt d)$ converge to those of $\mathrm{He}_k(z)/\sqrt{k!}$, and a second application of dominated convergence gives
\[
\mathbb E\bigl[\sigma(\sqrt d\,t)\,h_k(t)\bigr]\ \longrightarrow\ \frac{\mathbb E[\sigma(z)\mathrm{He}_k(z)]}{\sqrt{k!}}=c_k .
\]
By \eqref{eq:general-Nksigmak}, $N_k\sigma_k^2\to c_k^2$. Since $N_k\asymp d^k$, this gives $\sigma_k^2\asymp d^{-k}$ when $c_k\ne0$.

\emph{(iii)} The law of $t$ is symmetric, so $P_k(-t)=(-1)^kP_k(t)$. If $\sigma$ is odd and $k$ is even, the function $t\mapsto\sigma(\sqrt d\,t)P_k(t)$ is odd, and $\sigma_k=0$ by \eqref{eq:general-sigmak}. The case of $\sigma$ even and $k$ odd is the same.

name: Quadratic improvement for general activations

title: Proof
body_md:
All constants below depend only on $\sigma$, $\alpha$, and $k_0$, and $d$ is taken large enough.

\emph{Step 1: $\nu\asymp d^{-\alpha}$.} Since $\sigma_k^2/(\sigma_k^2+\nu)\le\sigma_k^2/\nu$, the fixed point \eqref{eq:main-fixed-point} gives
\[
d^\alpha=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{N_k\sigma_k^2}{\sigma_k^2+\nu}\le\frac{\operatorname{tr}\Psi}{\nu},
\qquad\text{so}\qquad
\nu\lesssim d^{-\alpha}
\]
by Lemma~\ref{lem:general-coefficients}(i). For the lower bound we keep only the degree $k_\star$:
\[
d^\alpha\ \ge\ \frac{N_{k_\star}\sigma_{k_\star}^2}{\sigma_{k_\star}^2+\nu}.
\]
If $\nu\le\sigma_{k_\star}^2$, the right-hand side is at least $N_{k_\star}/2\asymp d^{k_\star}$, which exceeds $d^\alpha$ because $k_\star>\alpha$. Hence $\nu>\sigma_{k_\star}^2$, and
\[
\nu\ \ge\ \frac{N_{k_\star}\sigma_{k_\star}^2}{2\,d^\alpha}\ \gtrsim\ d^{-\alpha},
\]
since $N_{k_\star}\sigma_{k_\star}^2\to c_{k_\star}^2>0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:general-coefficients}(ii). This is the argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:nu-relu}.

\emph{Step 2: the teacher.} Write $\lambda=\sigma_{k_0}^2$ and $L=\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm TE}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:general-coefficients}(ii), $\lambda\asymp d^{-k_0}$. For a unit target of degree $k_0$, \eqref{eq:main-teacher} and Step~1 give
\[
L=\frac{\nu}{\lambda+\nu}\ \asymp\ \min\{1,\,d^{k_0}\nu\}\ \asymp\ d^{-(\alpha-k_0)_+}.
\]

\emph{Step 3: the student.} The lower bound $\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm ST}(T)\ge L^2$ is Theorem~\ref{theo:quadratic-floor}. For the upper bound we bound the two terms of \eqref{eq:main-two-term}. The choice of $T$ gives $e^{-\lambda T}=L/m$, so the squared bias is
\[
\overline B(T)=\Bigl(\frac{\nu+\lambda e^{-\lambda T}}{\lambda+\nu}\Bigr)^2
=L^2\Bigl(1+\frac{1-L}{m}\Bigr)^2\le 4L^2 .
\]
In the variance, the prefactor is $\nu\lambda/(\lambda+\nu)^2=L(1-L)\le L$, so
\[
\overline V(T)\le L\,R(T),
\qquad
R(T)=\frac{\operatorname{tr}[\Psi(\Psi+\nu I)^{-2}(I-e^{-\Psi T})^2]}{\operatorname{tr}[\Psi(\Psi+\nu I)^{-2}]}\le1 .
\]
If $\alpha\le k_0$, then $L\asymp1$, and $\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm ST}(T)\le4L^2+L\lesssim L^2$.

Let $\alpha>k_0$. It remains to show that $R(T)\lesssim L$. In the denominator we keep only the degree $k_\star$. Since $\sigma_{k_\star}^2\asymp d^{-k_\star}\le\nu$,
\[
\operatorname{tr}[\Psi(\Psi+\nu I)^{-2}]\ \ge\ \frac{N_{k_\star}\sigma_{k_\star}^2}{(\sigma_{k_\star}^2+\nu)^2}\ \ge\ \frac{N_{k_\star}\sigma_{k_\star}^2}{4\nu^2}\ \gtrsim\ \nu^{-2}.
\]
In the numerator, we bound the degrees $k\le k_0$ using $(1-e^{-xT})^2\le1$ and $x/(x+\nu)^2\le1/(4\nu)$, and the degrees $k>k_0$ using $(1-e^{-xT})^2\le x^2T^2$ and $x^2/(x+\nu)^2\le1$. This gives
\[
\operatorname{tr}[\Psi(\Psi+\nu I)^{-2}(I-e^{-\Psi T})^2]
\ \le\ \sum_{k\le k_0}\frac{N_k}{4\nu}+T^2\sum_{k>k_0}N_k\sigma_k^2
\ \lesssim\ \frac{d^{k_0}}{\nu}+d^{2k_0}(\log d)^2,
\]
where we used $\operatorname{tr}\Psi\lesssim1$ and $T=\lambda^{-1}\log(m/L)\lesssim d^{k_0}\log d$. Dividing, and using $\nu\asymp d^{-\alpha}$ and $k_0<\alpha$,
\[
R(T)\ \lesssim\ \nu^2\Bigl(\frac{d^{k_0}}{\nu}+d^{2k_0}(\log d)^2\Bigr)
\ \asymp\ d^{-(\alpha-k_0)}+d^{-2(\alpha-k_0)}(\log d)^2
\ \lesssim\ d^{-(\alpha-k_0)}\ \asymp\ L .
\]
Hence $\overline V(T)\lesssim L^2$, and $\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm ST}(T)=\overline B(T)+\overline V(T)\lesssim L^2$.

label: ex:general-relu
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:general-relu}
Let $\sigma(r)=r_+$, and let $\varphi$ be the standard Gaussian density. Two integrations by parts, using $\mathrm{He}_k\varphi=-(\mathrm{He}_{k-1}\varphi)'$, give
\[
\mathbb E[z_+\mathrm{He}_k(z)]=\varphi(0)\,\mathrm{He}_{k-2}(0),\qquad k\ge2,
\]
which vanishes exactly when $k$ is odd. Hence $\mathcal K_\sigma=\{0,1\}\cup2\mathbb N=\mathcal K$, with $c_0^2=1/(2\pi)$ and $c_1^2=1/4$, and Theorem~\ref{theo:general-activation} recovers Theorem~\ref{theo:weaktostrongrelu}. The coefficients $\sigma_k$ with $k\ge3$ odd vanish exactly at every $d$, by Lemma~\ref{lem:general-coefficients}(iii): $r_+-r/2=|r|/2$ is even, and the linear part $r/2$ contributes only to degree one.
head: environment
name: ReLU

label: ex:general-tanh
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:general-tanh}
Let $\sigma=\tanh$. We show that $\mathcal K_\sigma$ is the set of odd integers. Since $\tanh$ is odd, $c_k=0$ for every even $k$, and $\sigma_k=0$ exactly at every even degree by Lemma~\ref{lem:general-coefficients}(iii). Let $k$ be odd. One Gaussian integration by parts gives
\[
\mathbb E[\tanh(z)\mathrm{He}_k(z)]=\mathbb E[\operatorname{sech}^2(z)\mathrm{He}_{k-1}(z)].
\]
The function $\operatorname{sech}^2$ has a positive, integrable Fourier transform,
\[
\operatorname{sech}^2(r)=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\pi\xi}{\sinh(\pi\xi/2)}\,e^{i\xi r}\,d\xi,
\]
and $\mathbb E[e^{i\xi z}\mathrm{He}_{k-1}(z)]=(i\xi)^{k-1}e^{-\xi^2/2}$. Exchanging the order of integration, and using that $k-1$ is even,
\[
\mathbb E[\tanh(z)\mathrm{He}_k(z)]
=\frac{(-1)^{(k-1)/2}}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}\xi^{k-1}\,\frac{\pi\xi}{\sinh(\pi\xi/2)}\,e^{-\xi^2/2}\,d\xi .
\]
The integrand is positive, so $c_k\ne0$, with sign $(-1)^{(k-1)/2}$. Hence Theorem~\ref{theo:general-activation} applies to every odd target degree $k_0$ and every $\alpha>0$:
\[
\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm TE}\asymp d^{-(\alpha-k_0)_+},\qquad
\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm ST}(T)\asymp\overline{\mathcal L}_{\rm TE}^{\,2},
\]
exactly as for ReLU. For an even target degree nothing is learned, by Remark~\ref{rem:general-activation-scope}. The argument uses only that $\sigma$ is odd and that $\sigma'$ has a nonnegative Fourier transform that is not identically zero; it applies, for instance, to $\sigma=\operatorname{erf}$.

name: tanh

label: ex:general-sigmoid
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:general-sigmoid}
Let $s(r)=1/(1+e^{-r})=\tfrac12+\tfrac12\tanh(r/2)$. The function $s-\tfrac12$ is odd, and the constant $\tfrac12$ contributes only to degree zero. Hence $c_0=\tfrac12$ and $c_k=0$ for every even $k\ge2$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:general-coefficients}(iii) also $\sigma_k=0$ for every even $k\ge2$ and every $d$. For odd $k$, the argument of Example~\ref{ex:general-tanh} applies with $\operatorname{sech}^2$ replaced by $s'(r)=\tfrac14\operatorname{sech}^2(r/2)$, whose Fourier transform $\pi\xi/\sinh(\pi\xi)$ is again positive. Hence $\mathcal K_s$ consists of $0$ and the odd integers, and the conclusions of Example~\ref{ex:general-tanh} hold unchanged.

A bias breaks the parity. For the activation $r\mapsto s(r+b)$, the same computation gives, for $k\ge1$,
\[
\mathbb E[s(z+b)\mathrm{He}_k(z)]=\frac1{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{\pi\xi}{\sinh(\pi\xi)}\,e^{i\xi b}\,(i\xi)^{k-1}e^{-\xi^2/2}\,d\xi .
\]
As a function of $b$ this extends to an entire function. For odd $k$ it is nonzero at $b=0$, and for even $k$ its derivative at $b=0$ is nonzero by the same positivity. So it is not identically zero and has countably many real zeros. Therefore, for all $b$ outside a countable set, $c_k\ne0$ for every $k$, and Theorem~\ref{theo:general-activation} applies to targets of every degree $k_0\ge1$.
